Italy.text: In AD 92 Emperor Domitian had a great many vineyards destroyed, to free up land for food.
Italy.evidence: Under ancient Rome large-scale, slave-run plantations sprang up in many coastal areas of Italy and spread to such an extent that, in AD 92, Emperor Domitian was forced to destroy a great number of vineyards in order to free up fertile land for food production.

France.text: Its winemaking began in the 6th century BCE, with the Greek settlers who founded Marseille.
France.evidence: French wine originated in the 6th century BCE, with the colonization of Southern Gaul by Greek settlers. Viticulture soon flourished with the founding of the Greek colony of Marseille.

Spain.text: It has more land under vines than any other country, over 1.2 million hectares, but its old vines yield little.
Spain.evidence: Spain has over 1.2 million hectares (3.0 million acres) planted in wine grapes, making it the most widely planted wine-producing nation, but the third largest producer of wine in the world, behind Italy and France and ahead of the United States; this is due, in part, to the very low yields and wide spacing of the old vines

United States.text: Prohibition nearly ended its wine industry; before it, dry wines outsold sweet ones three to one.
United States.evidence: Following the Repeal of Prohibition in 1933, operators tried to revive the American wine-making industry, which was nearly ended. ... Before Prohibition, dry table wines outsold sweet wines by three to one, but afterward, the ratio of demand changed dramatically.

China.text: One region, Yantai-Penglai, with over 140 wineries, makes 40% of its wine.
China.evidence: The largest producing region is Yantai-Penglai; with over 140 wineries, it produces 40% of China's wine.

Australia.text: Its first vines came from the Cape of Good Hope on the First Fleet, in 1788.
Australia.evidence: Vine cuttings from the Cape of Good Hope were brought to the penal colony of New South Wales by Governor Phillip on the First Fleet (1788).

Chile.text: The phylloxera louse that ravaged Europe's vines never reached it, so its vines need no grafting.
Chile.evidence: Chile is also fortunate to remain free of the phylloxera louse, which means that its grapevines do not require grafting with phylloxera-resistant rootstocks.

Argentina.text: Mendoza province alone makes more than 60% of its wine.
Argentina.evidence: The Mendoza province produces more than 60% of the Argentine wine and is the source of an even higher percentage of the total exports.

South Africa.text: Its first wine was made in Cape Town in 1659, by the colony's founder Jan van Riebeeck.
South Africa.evidence: South African wine has a history dating back to 1659, with the first bottle being produced in Cape Town by its founder and governor Jan van Riebeeck.

Portugal.text: Two of its wine regions are UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Douro Valley and Pico Island.
Portugal.evidence: Portugal has two wine-producing regions protected by UNESCO as World Heritage: the Douro Valley Wine Region (Douro Vinhateiro) and Pico Island Wine Region (Ilha do Pico Vinhateira).
